title-group.article-title: Assessing Nitrogen Oxide Dispersion From a Natural Gas Compressor Station to Support Sustainable Energy Infrastructure Operation

contrib-group.aff: School of Advanced Technologies, Iran University of Science and Technology, 1684613114 Tehran, Iran

abstract.p: Nitrogen oxide emissions from gas turbines at natural gas compressor stations pose a local environmental challenge to the sustainable operation of energy infrastructure. This study assesses nitrogen oxide dispersion around the Marand natural gas compressor station in northwestern Iran to identify candidate areas for ambient monitoring. Stack measurements from three natural gas-fired turbines were compiled to characterize nitric oxide (NO), nitrogen dioxide (NO$_2$), and total nitrogen oxides (NO$_x$). Meteorological data were processed using American Meteorological Society/Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model Improvement Committee Meteorological Preprocessor (AERMET), and dispersion was simulated using the American Meteorological Society/U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model (AERMOD). Maximum 1-hour and 24-hour concentrations were compared together with their receptor coordinates and occurrence times. The predicted maximum 1-hour concentrations of NO, NO$_2$, and NO$_x$ were 90.50, 5.07, and 91.72 μg/m$^3$, respectively; the corresponding maximum 24-hour concentrations were 11.56, 0.88, and 11.71 μg/m$^3$. The hourly peak receptors were closely grouped, whereas the daily NO$_2$ and NO$_x$ peak receptors were approximately 0.70 km from their respective hourly peak locations. The NO peak receptor remained unchanged between averaging periods. These results indicate that selecting monitoring locations from an hourly maximum alone may overlook locations associated with the highest daily concentrations. Joint interpretation of peak magnitude, location, and timing identifies candidate monitoring areas and provides information relevant to the environmental management and sustainable operation of natural gas transmission infrastructure.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p:
Reducing emissions at the combustor and assessing their consequences in the surrounding atmosphere address different parts of this problem. Combustion controls act on pollutant formation and release, whereas dispersion assessment examines the concentrations resulting from those releases under specified atmospheric conditions. Technical assessments of natural gas combustion turbines describe several approaches to NO
x
control, with applicability depending on turbine design and operating conditions [2]. However, stack measurements alone cannot identify the locations of maximum ground-level concentrations. Exhaust temperature and velocity affect plume behavior, while atmospheric transport and turbulent mixing determine how pollutants reach surrounding receptors. A spatial assessment is therefore needed to connect source conditions with monitoring priorities outside the facility.

American Meteorological Society/U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model (AERMOD) is an established tool for examining this connection. Its formulation represents dispersion from industrial sources through atmospheric boundary-layer characteristics and treatments of plume behavior and terrain [3]. Evidence from model comparisons supports its use while also demonstrating the importance of application conditions. Jittra et al. [4] evaluated AERMOD and California Puff Model using emissions from 292 industrial point sources and observations at ten monitoring sites in Thailand. AERMOD performed better overall for the pollutants assessed, including the upper end of the concentration distribution. This comparison supports the selection of AERMOD for industrial dispersion assessment, but its outcome does not imply equivalent predictive performance for every source configuration or meteorological setting.

Studies in Iran show how source measurements and dispersion modeling can be combined to investigate emissions from energy and process facilities. Hallaji et al. [5] measured pollutants from seven olefin-plant stacks and coupled AERMOD with meteorological fields from the Weather Research and Forecasting model. Their analysis related the orientation of concentration contours to prevailing winds, demonstrating that the spatial consequences of emissions cannot be inferred from stack concentrations alone. Mousavi et al. [6] examined CO, CO
2
, and SO
2
dispersion from refinery flares under continuous and non-continuous operation. Although flare releases differ from turbine exhausts, that study illustrates why operating conditions must be considered when interpreting facility-related concentration patterns. Together, these applications establish a useful methodological basis without providing concentration estimates transferable directly to a natural gas compressor station.

More recent work has placed greater emphasis on the quality and interpretation of the emissions supplied to dispersion models. Rivero et al. [7] combined mobile miniature differential optical absorption spectroscopy (mini-differential optical absorption spectroscopy) measurements collected during seven campaigns between 2022 and 2024 with AERMOD simulations of the Tula industrial complex in Mexico. Their approach connected measured emission fluxes with the distribution of pollutants around nearby communities. Emerson and Khan [8] subsequently incorporated probabilistic emission inputs into an AERMOD screening framework, using a virtual pulp mill to examine the implications of emission variability. These studies address different source types and assessment objectives, but both show that a concentration estimate needs to be understood in relation to the emissions and conditions it represents. This is also relevant to compressor stations, where measurements from individual turbines provide the source-specific basis for assessing their combined atmospheric contribution.

The spatial interpretation of model outputs is equally important. A concentration at one receptor does not necessarily characterize the surrounding area, particularly for pollutants with strong local gradients. Fang et al. [9] demonstrated that spatial representativeness affected the evaluation of modeled NO
2
against ground observations. Their study concerned chemical transport models rather than station-scale plume modeling, but it identifies a broader assessment issue: the spatial support of an observation or prediction must match the question being addressed. For a compressor station, reporting only the largest concentration omits the receptor location that makes the result useful for monitoring.

Monitoring studies also show that sampling design affects the information obtained from an observation network. Blanco et al. [10] evaluated how the design of mobile monitoring campaigns influenced air pollution exposure models, emphasizing the relationship between sampling coverage and the resulting predictions. A station-level dispersion assessment serves a more focused purpose: it can identify candidate locations for examining the modeled contribution of a particular facility. For that purpose, both concentration magnitude and averaging period matter. The highest hourly concentration describes a short-duration peak, whereas a daily maximum reflects concentrations averaged over a longer interval. Their locations need not coincide, so a monitoring location selected from one statistic may not represent the other.

The practical question at the Marand natural gas compressor station is therefore not simply whether NO
x
disperse beyond the stacks, but where the largest predicted concentrations occur and whether those locations remain consistent across pollutants and averaging periods. Addressing this question requires the source measurements, concentration maps, and numerical receptor outputs to be interpreted together. This approach gives the assessment a specific operational use: identifying the spatial features that a monitoring plan should examine.

This study assesses nitric oxide (NO), NO
2
, and NO
x
dispersion around the Marand natural gas compressor station in northwestern Iran using measurements from three natural gas-fired turbines and AERMOD simulations driven by meteorological data processed with American Meteorological Society/Environmental Protection Agency Regulatory Model Improvement Committee Meteorological Preprocessor (AERMET). The analysis compares maximum 1-hour and 24-hour concentrations, identifies their receptor locations and occurrence times, and examines whether the spatial focus of the predicted peaks changes with the averaging period. Its contribution is the joint interpretation of peak magnitude, location, and timing to inform ambient monitoring around the station. By connecting measured turbine emissions with specific monitoring priorities, the assessment supports the environmental management and sustainable operation of natural gas transmission infrastructure.

sec.title: 2.1. Study site and source characteristics
sec.p: The study examined the Marand natural gas compressor station in East Azerbaijan Province, northwestern Iran. The station maintains pressure within the natural gas transmission network. Three natural gas-fired turbines, designated C, D, and E, were included in the dispersion assessment. Their exhaust stacks constituted the emission sources considered in the analysis of nitrogen oxide concentrations around the facility.

The station was located at 38.517565° N, 45.357283° E. Each exhaust stack had an internal diameter of 2.00 m. Sampling points were positioned 10 m above the gas entry point, while the stack outlets were 14 m above the same reference. The exhaust conditions associated with the measurements are summarized in Table 1.

caption.title: Exhaust conditions of the three gas turbines

sec.title: 2.2. Stack measurements and pollutant data
sec.p:
Emission data were compiled from laboratory measurements of the three turbine exhausts. The measurement reports identified a Testo 340 flue gas analyzer and provided values for NO, NO
2
, NO
x
, SO
2
, CO, CO
2
, and O
2
. The nitrogen oxide measurements formed the focus of the dispersion assessment, while the remaining components described the accompanying exhaust composition.

Reported exhaust gas concentrations are presented in Table 2. NO and NO
2
were examined individually, while NO
x
represented the total nitrogen oxide quantity reported in the measurement dataset. NO
x
was thus distinguished from its constituent species rather than interpreted as an additional independent chemical compound.

The measurement dataset also contained oxygen-corrected mass concentrations at a reference oxygen content of 15% (Table 3). These values were presented separately from the measured volumetric concentrations in Table 2. They describe exhaust conditions and were not treated as ambient concentrations or used to infer pollutant composition at the peak receptors.

The reported gas concentrations and oxygen-corrected values were used to characterize the exhaust composition of the three turbines. These source measurements were distinguished from the receptor concentrations predicted by AERMOD. Comparisons among turbines were restricted to the measured exhaust characteristics; turbine-specific contributions to ambient concentrations were not inferred from stack concentrations alone.

sec.title: 2.3. Meteorological data and processing
sec.p: Meteorological information for the station surroundings was obtained from Solcast. The variables included air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, wind direction, and atmospheric pressure. Bright [11] evaluated Solcast’s historical solar irradiance product; that validation does not establish the accuracy of the meteorological variables used here.

caption.title: Reported exhaust pollutant concentrations corrected to 15% reference oxygen

sec.p: Meteorological data were processed using AERMET for the AERMOD simulations. AERMET produces surface and profile files that describe the atmospheric conditions used in dispersion calculations [12]. Wind direction, wind speed, and boundary-layer turbulence influence transport and dilution within this framework.

The present analysis examined the resulting receptor concentrations and peak locations. Separate sensitivity calculations were not conducted to quantify the effects of individual meteorological variables.

sec.title: 2.4. Atmospheric dispersion assessment
sec.p:
AERMOD predictions were evaluated to characterize the spatial distribution of NO, NO
2
, and NO
x
around the station. AERMOD uses a steady-state plume formulation based on atmospheric boundary-layer turbulence and scaling relationships [3], [13].

The analysis used source-group concentration summaries and receptor-specific contour maps. The numerical summaries provided ranked concentrations, projected receptor coordinates, and occurrence times. The contour maps were examined alongside these summaries to relate concentration magnitudes to their spatial distributions. Individual turbine contributions were not estimated.

NO, NO
2
, and NO
x
outputs were examined separately. The NO
2
values were interpreted as predictions conditional on the model configuration, rather than as an independently verified representation of total ambient NO
2
. Differences among the outputs were not used to quantify atmospheric conversion between NO and NO
2
.

Comparisons of concentration magnitude were made within a common averaging period. Independently selected pollutant maxima were not added because their receptor locations could differ. The contour maps represented the highest 1-hour concentration at each receptor over the modeled period, rather than a single plume occurring simultaneously throughout the domain.

sec.title: 3.1. Predicted concentrations across averaging periods
sec.p:
The maximum predicted concentrations differed among pollutants and averaging periods (Table 4). The highest 1-hour concentrations of NO, NO
2

3

sec.title: 3.2. Spatial distribution of maximum hourly concentrations
sec.p:
Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3 present the spatial distributions of the highest 1-hour concentrations of NO, NO
2
, and NO
x
. Each distribution contained a localized high-concentration zone surrounded by lower concentration contours. The contours were asymmetric, and the gradients differed around the high-value zones. The concentration field therefore could not be described as a uniform decline with distance from the station. Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3 retain the original concentration contours, with reformatted labels and coordinate axes approximately reconstructed from the original graphical outputs. Quantitative comparisons use the numerical model summaries.

The NO map showed a compact maximum within a broader area of lower concentrations (Figure 1). The NO
2
maximum occurred in the same general part of the modeled domain, although the associated concentration scale was substantially lower (Figure 2). The NO
x
map also placed its highest concentration within this area (Figure 3). The three maps showed a broadly consistent spatial focus for hourly peaks, while the numerical summaries identified the corresponding receptor coordinates.

The maps used different concentration scales. Similar colors across the figures consequently did not indicate equal concentrations, and differences in mapped contour extent were interpreted with reference to the numerical legend for each pollutant. The highest 1-hour distributions also represented receptor-specific maxima over the modeled period rather than a single simultaneous plume. The timing of the overall maxima was therefore examined separately.

sec.title: 4.1. Interpretation of concentration magnitudes and spatial patterns
sec.p: The simulations identified localized concentration maxima rather than a uniform decline with distance from the station. This distinction is important for elevated turbine exhausts: the release point and the location of the highest ground-level concentration need not coincide. Plume rise and atmospheric mixing determine where an elevated release reaches ground-level receptors, while interactions with nearby structures can modify its dispersion. Research on AERMOD building downwash and plume rise has demonstrated the sensitivity of near-source predictions to these processes [14]. Evaluations of highly buoyant plumes have shown that the treatment of plume penetration and subsequent mixing into the convective boundary layer can affect predicted ground-level concentrations [15]. These mechanisms provide a physical context for the asymmetric patterns at Marand, although the present results do not isolate their individual contributions.

The similarity between the maximum NO and NO
x
concentrations was consistent with the predominance of NO in the measured exhaust composition. However, this agreement should not be interpreted as a quantitative determination of ambient nitrogen oxide speciation. The independently ranked maxima occurred at different receptors, and the NO
x
reporting basis must be considered when comparing mass concentrations. Under the modeled conditions, NO and NO
x
had similar peak concentrations, while the NO
2
maxima were lower.

The lower NO
2
predictions also require a distinction between directly emitted NO
2
and NO
2
formed after release. Atmospheric conversion depends on chemical interactions, including the reaction of NO with ozone and the photolysis of NO
2
. Carruthers et al. [16] showed that alternative chemical treatments within AERMOD produced different NO
2
predictions when evaluated against field datasets. Consequently, the comparatively low NO
2
values at Marand characterize the modeled concentration field; they do not establish that secondary NO
2
formation is unimportant.

sec.title: 4.2. Averaging period and the location of maximum concentrations
sec.p:
The comparison between averaging periods revealed information that was not apparent from concentration magnitude alone. Although the hourly peak receptors were closely grouped, the daily NO
2
and NO
x
maxima occurred approximately 0.70 km from their respective hourly peak receptors. The daily NO maximum remained at its hourly peak receptor. Thus, spatial agreement among pollutants depended on the averaging period.

This difference is physically plausible because hourly and daily maxima represent different temporal selections. An hourly maximum can arise from a brief combination of transport and mixing conditions, whereas a daily maximum reflects concentrations averaged over a 24-hour interval. A receptor experiencing the largest single-hour concentration need not experience the largest daily average. The Marand outputs demonstrated this distinction directly through the coordinates associated with each maximum. They did not, however, establish which meteorological sequence produced the change in peak location.

The peak ratios provide a complementary description. Maximum hourly concentrations were approximately 7.83 times the daily maxima for NO and NO
x
and 5.78 times the daily maximum for NO
2
. These ratios summarize the contrast between two assessment metrics. They are not measures of concentration variability at a fixed location, nor do they indicate how frequently peak conditions occurred. Their practical value lies in showing that one averaging period cannot substitute for the other when describing the upper end of the predicted concentration field.

The three hourly maxima occurred during the same reported hour, whereas the daily maxima differed in occurrence date and receptor location. This combination shows why peak magnitude, position, and timing should be retained together. Reporting only the largest concentration would conceal whether different pollutants or averaging periods identify the same area for further investigation.

sec.title: 4.3. Comparison with related industrial and compressor station studies
sec.p: The Marand findings are consistent with the broader observation that industrial concentration patterns depend on source characteristics and atmospheric transport. Hallaji et al. [5] linked the orientation of modeled concentration contours around an Iranian olefin plant to prevailing winds. Rivero et al. [7] combined measured emissions with dispersion modeling to identify communities affected by an industrial complex in Mexico. The present assessment focused on three turbine stacks at a natural gas compressor station and compared the receptor locations associated with hourly and daily concentration maxima.

Direct numerical comparisons with those facilities would be misleading without harmonizing emission rates, stack conditions, receptor arrangements, meteorological periods, and pollutant treatment. A lower predicted concentration at Marand cannot by itself establish cleaner turbine operation or superior environmental performance. The useful comparison concerns the assessment approach: source measurements describe emissions, while dispersion outputs locate their potential atmospheric consequences.

Compressor station research provides a particularly relevant basis for interpreting model reliability. Panek et al. [17] evaluated AERMOD at a natural gas compressor station using concurrent emissions, meteorology, ambient NO
x
, and ozone measurements collected over 13 months. Their analysis showed that assumptions about emissions and meteorological inputs could materially affect modeled-to-observed comparisons. Although that station used reciprocating engines rather than the gas turbines assessed here, the study demonstrates why general acceptance of a dispersion model does not establish its accuracy for an individual facility.

The contribution of the Marand analysis is site-specific: it identifies differences in peak magnitude, receptor location, and occurrence time between hourly and daily concentration metrics. These comparisons provide information for selecting candidate monitoring areas around the station.

sec.title: 4.4. Implications for monitoring and sustainable operation
sec.p:
The separation between hourly and daily peak locations identifies candidate areas for subsequent monitoring assessment. A location selected solely from the hourly NO
x
maximum would not coincide with the predicted daily NO
2
or NO
x
maximum. The hourly and daily peak areas therefore warrant joint examination before selecting monitoring locations.

These modeled locations should guide an initial screening of monitoring options rather than determine an installation layout on their own. Final placement also depends on access, site boundaries, instrument exposure, nearby obstructions, and the monitoring objective. A monitoring site intended to investigate short-duration peaks may require a different placement strategy from one intended to characterize daily concentrations or background conditions.

This interpretation agrees with monitoring research showing that sampling design affects the information obtained from an observation network [10]. Liu et al. [18] further demonstrated, for coal-port operations, that accounting for uncertain operational and wind conditions could improve the robustness of monitoring layouts. Their optimization method was not applied in the present study, but it supports the principle that monitoring decisions should consider more than one concentration scenario.

For Marand, the results support consideration of both peak areas, potentially through an initial mobile campaign or a combination of fixed and temporary measurements. Such measurements could establish whether the modeled spatial distinction persists under actual operating conditions.

The relevance to sustainable operation lies in directing environmental observations toward locations where elevated station-related concentrations are predicted. Measurements at these locations could establish a baseline for evaluating subsequent operational or emission-control changes.

sec.title: 4.5. Uncertainty and applicability
sec.p: The predictions are conditional on the source characteristics, meteorological inputs, and dispersion assumptions. Stack measurements describe the sampled operating conditions, whereas turbine utilization and emissions may vary over time. Emerson’s probabilistic assessment [8] illustrates how emission variability can be incorporated into AERMOD screening. The Marand results should therefore be interpreted as concentration patterns associated with the assessed conditions rather than as a complete description of all operating states.

The assessment focuses on the interpretation of the concentration outputs. Full reproduction of the dispersion calculations requires source-specific mass emission rates, concentration conversion conventions, the meteorological processing configuration, receptor-grid specifications, and the treatment of NO-to-NO
2
conversion. These elements are not fully documented in the present study. The results therefore support comparisons within the evaluated model outputs, while absolute concentrations and monitoring locations require further verification before operational or regulatory application.

The representation of plume behavior and meteorology also affects predictive performance. Pandey et al. [19] found that incorporating aircraft plume rise and shoreline meteorology improved agreement between AERMOD predictions and observations around Los Angeles airport. Although those conditions differ from the Marand compressor station, their evaluation demonstrates the importance of matching model treatments to the physical setting. The asymmetric concentration patterns at Marand are consistent with spatially varying dispersion, but the present analysis does not isolate the effects of plume rise, atmospheric stability, or surrounding structures.

Interpretation also depends on the averaging period and assessment objective. Tan et al. [20] examined industrial contributions using hourly, daily, and annual AERMOD outputs, illustrating the different temporal scales relevant to facility-related air pollution. At Marand, the separation between hourly and daily peak receptors similarly shows why a single concentration statistic is insufficient for identifying monitoring priorities. Wu et al. [21] extended AERMOD simulations around liquefied natural gas terminals to health and equity assessment by combining concentration estimates with additional population and health information. Such applications demonstrate the wider relevance of near-source modeling, while also clarifying that the present concentration results alone do not establish population exposure or health effects.

Field observations are needed to evaluate whether the predicted high-concentration areas correspond to actual station-related patterns. Dehkhoda et al. [22] combined remote and in situ measurements with Hybrid Single-Particle Lagrangian Integrated Trajectory (HYSPLIT) simulations to examine industrial emissions and their transport toward surrounding areas. Their approach illustrates how complementary measurements can be used to investigate industrial emission patterns and their downwind influence. For Marand, concurrent nitrogen oxide, meteorological, and turbine operating measurements would allow the modeled hourly and daily peak areas to be examined under comparable conditions.

Monitoring around the station would require calibration and reference comparisons, particularly if compact sensor networks were used to extend spatial coverage. Studies of NO and NO
2
sensors have demonstrated the importance of deployment conditions, ozone interference, and scalable calibration procedures [23], [24]. Aleahmad et al. [25] combined AERMOD predictions with the analytic hierarchy process to select monitoring locations in an Iranian petrochemical zone. Their approach illustrates how dispersion outputs can be integrated with additional siting criteria; the peak locations identified at Marand represent an initial screening step rather than an optimized monitoring network.

Finally, peak coordinates identify the highest values among the receptors evaluated and do not establish the exact location of a continuous atmospheric maximum. NO
2
interpretation additionally depends on the treatment of atmospheric conversion [16], while ambient compliance assessment requires background concentrations and contributions from other sources. Within these boundaries, the results provide candidate monitoring areas and a basis for testing the station’s local air quality influence.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: This study assessed nitrogen oxide dispersion around the Marand natural gas compressor station using stack measurements from three gas turbines and AERMOD simulations. The analysis compared predicted concentration magnitudes, peak receptor locations, and occurrence times to identify candidate areas for ambient monitoring.

The maximum 1-hour concentrations of NO, NO
2
, and NO
x
were 90.50, 5.07, and 91.72 μg/m
3
, respectively, while the corresponding maximum 24-hour concentrations were 11.56, 0.88, and 11.71 μg/m
3
. The ratios of hourly to daily maxima were 7.83, 5.78, and 7.83, demonstrating the different concentration magnitudes represented by these averaging periods. The dispersion maps showed localized, asymmetric high-concentration zones rather than a uniform decrease with distance from the station.

The hourly maxima occurred at closely grouped receptors during the same reported hour. However, the daily NO
2
and NO
x
maxima occurred approximately 704 and 703 m from their respective hourly peak receptors, whereas the NO peak location remained unchanged. A location selected solely from an hourly maximum therefore did not coincide with every daily maximum.

The principal contribution is the joint interpretation of peak magnitude, location, and timing as a basis for monitoring decisions. For Marand, the hourly peak cluster and the separate daily NO
2
and NO
x
peak cluster identify candidate areas for further monitoring assessment. Their operational use requires confirmation of spatial resolution and comparison with ambient observations.

The findings describe the modeled station contribution under the assessed conditions. Their application to ambient air quality compliance requires consideration of background concentrations, NO-to-NO
2
conversion, and comparison with concurrent ambient observations.
